## Theory of risk and insurance 

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Condition of perfectly competitive market

- Many buyers and sellers

- A standardized product

- Mobile resources (free enter and exit the market)

- Perfect information
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Medical care differs in significant ways

- [Unpredictability]{.themec}

- Asymmetric information: 

  - A market situation where all participants do not have access to the
same level of information

- [Trust]{.themec}

  - Principal-agent problem (also a information asymmetric problem)

- Barriers to entry

- [Payment practices]{.themec}: Health insurance 
  
  - Moral hazard: the over use of health service due to health insurance

:::
::::

## How do we evaluate uncertainty (expected value)

### Example 1: 

> Currently, Elizabeth has $50,000 in her bank. it is estimated that Elizabeth has 4% of probability of incurring illness, which would cost her $50,000, what is Elizabeth expected income? 

$$E = R_1*P_1+R_2*P_2+R_3*P_3+ ...$$

$$E=R_1*P_1+R_2*P_2 = (50,000-50,000)*4\%+50,000*96\% = 48,000$$

### Example 2: 

> If the utility with $0 of income is 0, while the utility with $50,000 of income is 100, what is Elizabeth's expected utility?

$$E=R_1*P_1+R_2*P_2 = 0*4\%+100*96\% = 96$$

## How much are individuals willing to pay for health insurance

:::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Assumptions
  - Individuals make rational decisions
  - Individuals are risk averse, represented by diminishing turn of income or assets (Graph on the left)
- Concept (under uncertainty, no insurance)
  - Expected value under uncertainty  
      - $E = P_1*R_1+P_2*R_2+...+P_n*R_n$ 
  - Expected utility 
      - $U_e = 0*0.04+100*0.96=96$
  - Expected income
      - $I_e = 0*0.04+50,000*0.96=48,000$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

<center>

<img src="/pic/S9-F4.png" width="100%">

</center>

:::

::::

## How much health insurance company can charge (premium)

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

<center>

<img src="/pic/S9-F5.png" width="100%">

</center>

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

### Actuarially fair premium: 

- An actuarially fair premium is an insurance premium that is equal to the expected payout from the insurance company. 

- It's calculated by multiplying the probability of a claim by the amount of the claim

In the previous example, the actuarially fair premium = 4% * 50,000 = 2,000

:::
::::

---

## What do we learn from the exercixe 

- Insurance can be sold only in circumstances where the consumer is [risk averse]{.themec}.

- If insurance companies charge more than the actuarially fair premium, people will have less expected wealth from insuring than from not insuring.

- Even though people will have less wealth as a result of their purchases of insurance, the increased well-being comes from the [elimination of risk]{.themec}

- The willingness to buy insurance is related to the [distance]{.themec} between the utility curve and the expected utility line.

## Health insruance and market failure 

- Maral hazard

    - Third party payment $\rightarrow$ overuse of health care $\rightarrow$ moral hazard

- Adverse selection
    - Information problem (Asymmetry information) $\rightarrow$ adverse selection

---

## Moral Hazard

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

- Definition: Moral hazard occurs anytime there is an opportunity to gain from acting differently
from the implied principles of a contract

  - .themec[The contract changes consumer’s behaviors]

- Because private actions are hidden from view, both parties have an opportunity to gain from unpredictable behavior

- Having insurance:
  - Increases the likelihood of purchasing medical services
  - Induces higher spending in the event of illness
::: 

::: {.column width="50%"}

### The effect of moral hazard on medical care demand

## User fees and moral hazard

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

 - User charges can be viewed as a means of reducing moral hazard

  - Forms: co-payments, co-insurance, deductibles

  - Reduces utilization of health care by patients

- But there are problems:

  - Disproportionately affects lower income groups

  - Demand is reduced for effective treatments as well as trivial health care

  - May not reduce consumption if doctors induce demand
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}


<iframe width="450" height="300" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/kAKQ6TYzc-I" title="Why user fees won&#39;t make our health system more affordable, featuring Dr. Raisa Deber" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

:::
::::

## Adverse selection

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

- Adverse selection arises because
  - Individuals may have [better information]{.themec} of their risk status than does the insurance company
  - Individuals with a low risk of requiring health care may find it difficult to obtain ”actuarially fair” insurance – premium equal to expected cost of future consumption
  - Those with [lower risk]{.themec} will [not purchase insurance]{.themec} priced to cater for those with
average risk, whereas higher risk individuals will, SO…

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

- … average risk level of those remaining will
rise (as will premium) (continually)
- Result: those at [low risk]{.themec} (and high risk with
low income) [not insured]{.themec} (as premium rises)

<center> 

<img src = "/pic/S9-F7.png" width = "100%" />

</center> 

:::
::::

--- 

## Insurers' response to adverse selection
- Cream skimming: 
    - [‘experience rating’]{.themec} (set a different premium for different risk groups)
- Compulsory [public insurance]{.themec} 
    - Stops low risk leaving market (forced cross-subsidisation of those at high risk by those at low risk)

---

## Optimal insurance plan 

- Balances the benefits of greater risk sharing with the costs of moral hazard
- Make people responsible for more of their own care
- Requires higher deductibles and larger copays
- Pools high risk people into pools with other high risk people, and charges premiums
  to reflect that risk.

---

## State level insurance regulation

- Guaranteed issue
- Guaranteed renewability
- Restrictions on exclusions of pre-existing conditions
- Children < the age of 26 are covered under their parents’ plan

---

## The economics of mandates

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Mandates are not free
  - Mandates will have long term consequences on the ability of the health care system to
    provide access to quality care at affordable prices
  - In general, research indicates that mandates increase the costs of health care systems
  - Many working poor remain uninsured because state mandates make private insurance
    unaffordable for many
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

<center>

<img src = "/pic/S9-F8.png" width = "100%" />

</center>

:::
::::

## Relationship between insurance & Health

- Two parts to the connection:
    - How does lack of insurance affect access to medical care?
    - Does poor access result in poor health outcomes?
- Significant differences of opinion re whether lack of insurance leads to poor health
- Except for those who are poor and sick, there seems to be no relationship between
health status and insurance status
